turns.prompt_text: I would like to create a chrome or firefox extension for tabs. Right now, tabs are already improved by using groups, but I would like to take it a step further and use graphs / file structures. Essentially markdown header system, it doesn't need to be that deep, as markdown stops at about 7.
turns.response_html:
That is a killer concept. Moving from flat tab groups to a hierarchical, tree-structured, or graph-based system (like Markdown headers H1 through H6) makes perfect sense for deep-dive research or complex workflows.

Because both Chrome and Firefox use the standard WebExtensions API, you can build a cross-browser extension relatively easily. Here is a structural blueprint of how to architecture this extension.

🏗️ Core Architecture & Data Structure

To mimic a Markdown header system, you need a data structure that maps flat browser tabs to a parent-child tree.

1. The Data Model

Instead of relying purely on the browser's native tab ordering, you will maintain an internal state (stored in chrome.storage.local) that tracks the relationships.

{
  "tabId_101": { "id": 101, "level": 1, "parentId": null, "title": "Project Root" },
  "tabId_102": { "id": 102, "level": 2, "parentId": 101, "title": "Sub-topic (H2)" },
  "tabId_103": { "id": 103, "level": 3, "parentId": 102, "title": "Deep Dive (H3)" }
}

2. UI/UX Approaches

Standard horizontal tab strips cannot natively display a 6-to-7 level deep hierarchy. You have two primary options for the interface:

  • The Sidebar API (chrome.sidePanel or sidebar_action): This is the ideal UX. It gives you a vertical pane where you can render a collapsible tree view or indented list using standard HTML/CSS.
  • The Popup UI: A dropdown menu from the extension icon, though it closes when you click outside of it, making it less ideal for constant tab switching.

🛠️ Key WebExtension APIs You'll Need

1. manifest.json (The Blueprint)

You need to declare permissions to read tab data, intercept tab creation, and inject a sidebar.

{
  "manifest_version": 3,
  "name": "TabTree Markdown Headers",
  "version": "1.0",
  "permissions": ["tabs", "storage", "sidePanel"],
  "background": {
    "service_worker": "background.js"
  },
  "side_panel": {
    "default_path": "sidebar.html"
  }
}

2. background.js (The State Controller)

The background script monitors browser events and updates your hierarchical graph.

  • chrome.tabs.onCreated.addListener((tab) => { ... }) When a user opens a link in a new tab from an existing tab, you can intercept the tab.openerTabId. If an openerTabId exists, look up that parent's header level in your storage, and assign the new tab a level of parent.level + 1 (capped at 6 or 7).
  • chrome.tabs.onRemoved.addListener((tabId) => { ... }) If a parent tab (e.g., an H2) is closed, you must decide how to handle its children (H3+). You can either "promote" them up a level or close the entire sub-branch.

3. sidebar.js (The Visual Graph)

Your sidebar UI reads the state from chrome.storage.local and renders the tree dynamically.

  • Use simple CSS indentation based on the level: 
    .tab-level-1 { margin-left: 0px; font-weight: bold; }
.tab-level-2 { margin-left: 12px; }
.tab-level-3 { margin-left: 24px; }
  • Use chrome.tabs.update(tabId, { active: true }) when a user clicks a node in your sidebar to instantly jump to that tab.

🚀 Recommended Development Workflow

  1. Start with a Proof of Concept (PoC): Build just the sidePanel and populate it with a static hardcoded tree list. Ensure you can click an item and switch to an active tab.
  2. Implement Interception: Wire up the background.js listeners to detect when a tab is opened from a parent tab, and print the calculated "Markdown depth level" to the console.
  3. Sync State: Connect the background script's tracking logic to chrome.storage, and have the sidebar dynamically re-render whenever the storage changes using chrome.storage.onChanged.

Are you leaning toward a specific layout style for the UI, like a strict vertical file tree explorer, or something more fluid like a visual node graph?

turns.prompt_text: I wonder if anyone has already done this.
turns.response_html:
Yes, the core concept of nesting tabs hierarchically exists, and it actually has a cult following! In the browser extension world, this UI paradigm is widely known as "Tree Style Tabs."

Here is what the current landscape looks like:

The Big Players

  • Tree Style Tab (Firefox): This is the undisputed grandfather of the concept. It moves tabs to a vertical sidebar and automatically nests them. If you are on a Wikipedia page (Parent) and middle-click 5 links, those 5 new tabs open as indented "Children" under the parent. You can collapse the parent to hide the children.
  • Tree Style Tab Manager / Tab Tree (Chrome): Since Chrome added the sidePanel API, several extensions have replicated the Firefox experience. They render your active tabs as an expandable/collapsible file tree in the sidebar.
  • Tab Subgroups (Chrome): Instead of a sidebar tree, this extension hacks Chrome's native horizontal "Tab Groups" feature to allow nested folders (e.g., a "Work" group that contains a "Project A" subgroup).

How Your "Markdown" Angle is Different

Most existing "Tree" extensions act purely as a visual browsing history. They auto-generate the tree based on where you clicked from. If you go down a Wikipedia rabbit hole, you end up with a tree 15 levels deep that looks like a chaotic staircase.

Your idea of a Markdown Header System (H1 - H6) implies a much cleaner, more intentional organization—like an outliner document.

If you want to build this and stand out from the crowded "Tree Style Tab" market, you could focus on semantic, user-defined structure rather than automatic click-tracking:

  1. H1 Tabs are Workspaces: (e.g., "Trip to Japan", "Tax Returns").
  2. H2 / H3 Tabs are Sub-topics: You drag and drop tabs to indent them under the appropriate header, capping the visual depth at 6 or 7 so the UI doesn't break.
  3. Document View: Instead of just a file tree, you could literally render the sidebar to look like a Markdown outline, where clicking a header expands the tabs related to it.

turns.prompt_text: The barrier here is the ui, I don't know my constraints, I see for tab groups they've colored them and highlighted the top tab bar to show grouping, I wonder what is available to me to show representation. If I could I would increase the height of the entire tab area 4 times on mouse hover to really visualize the hierarchy of tabs
turns.response_html:
Manipulating the browser's native top tab strip is the biggest hurdle in modern extension development.

To save you from hitting a brick wall later, here is the honest truth about your constraints: Chrome and Firefox do not allow extensions to alter the native top tab bar's HTML, CSS, layout, or height. You cannot expand it on hover, change its height, or inject custom multi-layered rendering there. Chrome’s native tab groups are hardcoded into the browser's core C++ UI, not exposed via the WebExtensions API.

However, you still have powerful options to build a gorgeous, spatial visualization of your H1–H6 hierarchy. Here are the three main UI pathways available to you, along with their constraints and possibilities:

1. The Custom Top Bar (Using Content Scripts)

While you can't change the browser's actual tab bar, you can inject a custom HTML frame at the absolute top of every webpage the user visits.

  • How it works: Your extension injects a fixed div at the top of the viewport (position: fixed; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%;).
  • The Hover Trick: This does allow you to achieve your hover effect. By default, it could look like a thin line or a single row of "H1" titles. When the user hovers over it, you can transition its height dynamically using CSS (height: 180px;) to reveal a multi-tiered, spatial grid or graph of your sub-tabs (H2 down to H6).
  • The Constraints: It will sit on top of the web page content unless you programmatically shift the page's body down (margin-top: 180px;). It also has to reinject and rebuild its state every time the user navigates to a new URL.

2. The Sidebar API (sidePanel / sidebar_action)

This is the standard, most robust UI constraint path allowed by modern browsers. It gives you a dedicated vertical panel on the left or right side of the viewport.

  • What is available to you: Inside the sidebar, you are rendering a standard web page (sidebar.html). You have 100% control over the CSS and layout.
  • Representation Ideas: * The File Tree: A clean, indented layout where H1s look like folders, H2s are sub-folders, and individual tabs are files.
    • The Intentional Column View: A Miller Columns layout (like macOS Finder in column view). Clicking an H1 opens a second column showing its H2s, clicking an H2 opens a third column for H3s, and so on. This handles depth elegantly without cluttering the screen.
  • The Constraints: It eats into the horizontal screen real estate of the webpage, and users have to manually keep the sidebar open.

3. The "New Tab" Page Overwrite or Dashboard

Instead of managing tabs while browsing, you can take over the "New Tab" page or open a dedicated dashboard tab (e.g., chrome://extensions style but for your project).

  • What is available to you: A massive, full-screen canvas. You can use standard frontend libraries (like Tailwind, D3.js, or HTML Canvas) to build a massive spatial mind-map or infinite canvas graph of your tabs.
  • Representation Ideas: You can lay out your research visually like a Kanban board or an outline document where H1s are giant columns and sub-tabs stack vertically inside them.
  • The Constraints: It isn’t persistent; it’s a destination the user switches to when they want to organize, rather than a heads-up display that follows them around.

Architectural Verdict

If your heart is set on a horizontal, top-down spatial hierarchy that expands on hover, your best bet is exploring Option 1 (Injected Top Bar Content Script). If you want a reliable, clean, outliner-style UX that doesn't break page layouts, Option 2 (Sidebar) is the path of least resistance.

Which of those visual layouts feels closer to the workspace you are imagining for your tabs?

turns.response_html:
Building this as an extension that automatically tracks, archives, and visually scores your tabs over time is completely doable.

If you are dealing with dozens of tabs across multiple groups that vanish into the ether, what you need isn’t just a static tree view—you need an automated browser memory system. You want the extension to manage the clutter for you while building a longitudinal, visual map of your browsing habits over months.

Here is the strategy to build a personalized, automated archiving system using a hybrid approach: a background tracker + a dashboard/sidebar explorer.

🛠️ The Core Logic: The Background Script

To do the heavy lifting for you, the extension's background.js (Service Worker) will act as a silent archivist. It handles three core behaviors: Time-decay sleeping, Automated Archiving, and Interaction Scoring.

1. Tab Sleeping (Discarding)

You don't need to manually close or manage memory. The WebExtensions API has a built-in method called chrome.tabs.discard().

  • The Logic: If a tab hasn't been active for 30 minutes, the background script calls chrome.tabs.discard(tabId).
  • The Result: The tab stays visible in your visual list, but the browser completely frees up its RAM. When you click it again, it reloads instantly.

2. Interaction Scoring (The "Worth Going Back For" Metric)

Instead of just tracking a history of URLs, your extension will calculate a "Value Score" for every tab based on how you interacted with it. When a tab is created, it starts at Score = 0.

  • Time Spent: For every minute the tab is actively focused, add points (+5).
  • Scroll Depth: Did you actually read it? Track scroll events via a tiny content script (+10 if they scrolled past 50%).
  • Revisits: Did you return to this tab over multiple days? (+20 per distinct day).

3. Automated Archiving (The "Deeper" Archive)

Tabs shouldn't live in your active view forever.

  • The Rule: If a tab has a low Interaction Score and hasn't been looked at in 7 days, the extension automatically closes the browser tab but saves its metadata, hierarchy placement, and final score into chrome.storage.local.
  • The Outcome: Your actual browser stays clean, but your extension builds a long-term database of your internet footprint.

🗺️ The UI: Visualizing Months of Tabs

Because you want a deep, personalized visualization of your tabs over months, a massive full-screen dashboard (like the "New Tab" page or a pinned dashboard tab) gives you the spatial canvas you need. Here is how you can render your H1–H6 tab history:

The "Time-Layered Tree" Layout

Instead of a chaotic list, your dashboard can visualize tabs chronologically and hierarchically, prioritizing high-scoring tabs.

[Month: May 2026]
 └── H1: Project "Home Lab NAS Setup" (Score: 95) ★★★
      ├── H2: TrueNAS vs Unraid Hardware Guides (Score: 80)
      │    ├── H3: Optiplex idle power consumption thread (Score: 45)
      │    └── H3: ZFS pool layout calculator (Score: 90) [Auto-Archived]
      └── H2: 3D Printed HDD Brackets (Score: 15) -> [Faded/Small UI]

[Month: June 2026]
 └── H1: Smart Home RF Sensing Project (Score: 120) ★★★★
  • Visual Weight: High-scoring tabs are rendered in bold, vibrant colors or larger cards. Low-scoring tabs that were auto-archived appear faded, small, or collapsed.
  • One-Click Resurrection: Clicking any archived tab node immediately opens a fresh browser tab to that exact URL and restores its spot in the hierarchy.

🚀 How to Start Building This Week

To get this working without drowning in UI code upfront, you can build it in three iterative phases:

  • Phase 1: The Sensor (1-2 hours): Write the background.js script to listen to chrome.tabs.onActivated. Use performance.now() to log how long you spend on each tab into a simple console array.
  • Phase 2: The Auto-Sleeper (1 hour): Set up a chrome.alarms routine that loops through open tabs every 15 minutes and runs chrome.tabs.discard() on anything older than your cutoff.
  • Phase 3: The Data Canvas (3-4 hours): Create a basic dashboard.html page. Fetch all your saved tab objects from storage and render them as a simple, nested Markdown list on the page, sorted by the month they were created.

Once the data layer is tracking your scoring system accurately, we can hook it up to a highly customized visual outliner UI using standard HTML and CSS.

turns.prompt_text: Let me keep telling you about the problems I face. I open many tabs when I am working, then google runs out of memory and crashes, or over weeks a memory leak occurs and it crashes. If I could zoom out, have many levels of caching showing what I am using right this minute, this session/day, this week or two, and long term deep storage then I could have a better idea of where my time is going-spent and also keep better track of my projects and work.
turns.response_html:
What you are describing is a classic working memory collapse. Standard browsers treat all tabs as if they are equally important, forcing your computer's RAM to treat a deep-dive technical documentation page you haven't looked at in three days exactly the same as the document you are typing in right now.

To solve both the memory crashes and the cognitive overload, you can structure your extension around a Hierarchical Cache Architecture. Instead of just "open" or "closed," a tab should flow through four distinct physical and memory states based on your recency of use.

🧠 The 4-Tier Tab Cache Architecture

By mapping your tabs to a time-decay system, you create a visual and functional buffer that protects your computer's RAM while keeping your project history intact.

[ TIER 1: ACTIVE RAM ] -> Live tabs from the last 2 hours (Max 10-15 tabs)
         │
         ▼ (Time Decay / Inactivity)
[ TIER 2: SESSION CACHE ] -> Discarded from RAM via chrome.tabs.discard()
         │                   Still visible in browser bar, uses 0% CPU/Memory
         ▼ (End of Day / 24 Hours)
[ TIER 3: WEEKLY STAGING ] -> Closed in browser, moved to local storage
         │                    Visualized as active nodes in your H1-H6 dashboard
         ▼ (14+ Days Inactive)
[ TIER 4: DEEP ARCHIVE ] -> Cold storage. Compressed metadata & interaction scores
                             Searchable via visual mind-map/history explorer

Tier 1: Active Working Memory (Right Now)

  • What it is: Tabs you have interacted with in the last 0 to 2 hours.
  • The State: Fully loaded in RAM.
  • The Rules: If this tier exceeds 15 tabs, the extension throws a subtle visual warning or automatically pushes the lowest-scoring, oldest tab down to Tier 2 to prevent Chrome from hitting its memory ceiling.

Tier 2: The Session Sleep State (Today)

  • What it is: Tabs relevant to your current workday, but not looked at in the last few hours.
  • The State: Hibernated. The extension calls chrome.tabs.discard(tabId). The tab title and favicon remain perfectly visible in your browser tab strip or sidebar, but its memory footprint drops to zero.
  • The Trigger: Wakes up instantly when clicked.

Tier 3: Weekly Staging (The Dashboard Buffer)

  • What it is: The graveyard of your last 2 weeks of deep-dives, organized by your H1–H6 project structure.
  • The State: Evicted from the browser. The actual browser tabs are closed automatically by the background script after 24–48 hours of neglect, keeping your browser fast and free of memory leaks.
  • The Representation: They live on your full-screen extension dashboard. You can "zoom out" to see them grouped under project headers (e.g., Project: Home Lab Router Config). You can see exactly how many minutes you spent on them before they were evicted.

Tier 4: Long-Term Deep Storage (Months)

  • What it is: Your historical footprint.
  • The State: Text-compressed metadata strings stored in local indexedDB storage.
  • The Representation: A chronological timeline or zoomable graph. When you look at June 2026, you see a macro-view of your time allocation: "40% Embedded Systems Architecture, 20% Technical Documentation, 10% Local LLM Tooling."

🛠️ Preventing the Chrome Memory Crash

The reason Chrome crashes over weeks is usually a combination of JavaScript memory leaks on heavy, media-rich pages and the sheer volume of open processes.

By implementing Tier 2 (Auto-Discard) and Tier 3 (Auto-Eviction to Storage), you eliminate the source of the crash entirely:

  1. Garbage Collection: By letting the extension programmatically close tabs that are more than 48 hours old (after capturing their URL, Title, Hierarchy Level, and Score), you force Chrome to release that leaked memory back to your operating system.
  2. Infinite History: Because storage strings take up virtually no space compared to an active browser tab, you can store millions of historical hierarchy nodes in Tier 4 without ever lagging your machine.

If you like this multi-tiered caching mental model, we can map out the data-syncing lifecycle—specifically how a tab gracefully "steps down" from an active browser tab to a flat data node in your dashboard.

turns.response_html:
Let's lay down the foundational blueprint. To build a system that gracefully degrades tabs from Active RAM down to Deep Storage, we need a bulletproof architectural pipeline.

Here is the exact data lifecycle, the storage strategy, and the initial background logic needed to handle this multi-tiered caching system without crashing your browser.

💾 The Data Lifecycle Pipeline

Every time you open a tab, it enters a state machine managed by the extension. It flows through the tiers based on time and engagement.

1. The Tab Object Schema

To track hierarchy, time, and engagement, every tab is assigned a custom metadata object stored in the extension's local state:

{
  "id": "tab_unique_uuid_or_url_hash",
  "url": "https://news.ycombinator.com/",
  "title": "Hacker News",
  "tier": 1, 
  "hierarchy": {
    "level": 2,          // H2 tab
    "parentId": "parent_uuid_here",
    "rootProject": "Tech Research" // H1 level group
  },
  "metrics": {
    "totalActiveTimeMs": 1420000,  // ~23 minutes of active focus
    "lastAccessed": 1783724398000, // Timestamp
    "interactionScore": 85
  }
}

🏗️ Building Phase 1: The Core Background Engine

To prevent the exact memory leaks and crashes you are experiencing, the background service worker must monitor the browser and enforce Tier 2 (Sleeping) and Tier 3 (Staging) automatically.

Here is the structured implementation for your background.js:

// background.js

// Configuration Thresholds (Adjustable)
const TIER_2_SLEEP_TIMEOUT_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000; // 30 Minutes to Sleep
const TIER_3_EVICTION_TIMEOUT_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000; // 24 Hours to Archive & Close

// Keep track of which tab is active and when it was focused
let activeTabId = null;
let activeStartTime = Date.now();

// 1. TRACK ENGAGEMENT TIME
chrome.tabs.onActivated.addListener(async (activeInfo) => {
  const now = Date.now();
  
  // Save accrued time for the previous active tab before switching
  if (activeTabId !== null) {
    await updateTabActiveTime(activeTabId, now - activeStartTime);
  }
  
  activeTabId = activeInfo.tabId;
  activeStartTime = now;
});

// Helper to update active time in local storage
async function updateTabActiveTime(tabId, durationMs) {
  const data = await chrome.storage.local.get(['tabDatabase']);
  const db = data.tabDatabase || {};
  
  if (db[tabId]) {
    db[tabId].metrics.totalActiveTimeMs += durationMs;
    db[tabId].metrics.lastAccessed = Date.now();
    // Dynamically increase interaction score based on usage
    db[tabId].metrics.interactionScore += Math.floor(durationMs / 60000) * 5; 
    await chrome.storage.local.set({ tabDatabase: db });
  }
}

// 2. THE CACHE POLICEMAN (Runs every 15 minutes)
chrome.alarms.create("cacheEnforcer", { periodInMinutes: 15 });

chrome.alarms.onAlarm.addListener(async (alarm) => {
  if (alarm.name === "cacheEnforcer") {
    const now = Date.now();
    const tabs = await chrome.tabs.query({ currentWindow: true });
    const data = await chrome.storage.local.get(['tabDatabase']);
    const db = data.tabDatabase || {};

    for (let tab of tabs) {
      // Ignore the currently highlighted tab
      if (tab.active) continue;

      const tabMeta = db[tab.id];
      if (!tabMeta) continue;

      const idleTime = now - tabMeta.metrics.lastAccessed;

      // Tier 1 -> Tier 2: Hibernate if idle > 30 mins
      if (idleTime > TIER_2_SLEEP_TIMEOUT_MS && !tab.discarded) {
        chrome.tabs.discard(tab.id); 
        tabMeta.tier = 2;
        console.log(`[Tier 2] Hibernated Tab: ${tab.title} to save RAM.`);
      }

      // Tier 2 -> Tier 3: Evict from browser entirely if idle > 24 hours
      if (idleTime > TIER_3_EVICTION_TIMEOUT_MS) {
        tabMeta.tier = 3;
        // Keep the record in storage, but close the actual browser tab
        chrome.tabs.remove(tab.id);
        console.log(`[Tier 3] Evicted Tab: ${tab.title} to Dashboard Storage.`);
      }
    }
    
    await chrome.storage.local.set({ tabDatabase: db });
  }
});

📈 Next Up: The "Zoom Out" Visualizer

With this background architecture silently handling memory allocation, Chrome will stop crashing because your raw tab count will naturally hover around a tight, high-performance sweet spot (Tiers 1 & 2).

The real magic happens when we visualize Tier 3 (Staging) and Tier 4 (Archive) over weeks and months. To build a system where you can look back and actually see what's worth resurrecting, we need a dashboard UI layout.

This system must keep itself lean by enforcing a very low amount of tabs open at a time. Like a telescope, even though the context is large and or multi-contexed, only a small batch may be held in the hand actively
turns.response_html:
You hit the nail on the head. The "telescope" analogy is the perfect mental model for how a clean workflow should run: a massive visual field of view (the context), but a hyper-focused, incredibly narrow focal point of active execution (what's in your hand right now).

Your intuition about Chrome is also dead-on. It is incredibly invasive to aggressively crash or force-purge memory, and understanding why Chrome acts this way makes the case for your extension even stronger.

🛑 Why Doesn't Chrome Just "Detect" and Fix Leaks?

Chrome’s core engine (V8) uses an automated Garbage Collector (GC). The GC is a machine that sweeps through memory, looks for objects that have absolutely zero paths leading back to your active code, and vaporizes them.

The problem is that true technical memory leaks look exactly like legitimate intentional programming to a computer.

If a website developer writes a broken script where a closed widget is technically deleted from the screen, but it still has one single event listener attached to a hidden global object, Chrome's engine looks at it and thinks:

"Well, the user isn't interacting with this, but the code technically still has a path to it. If I delete this, I might completely break the webpage and crash the user's session."

Because Chrome values stability and speed above all else, it errs on the side of caution. It keeps the leaked object alive, assuming the code might need it later. Over weeks, those tiny stray references compound until the entire process hits a wall and collapses.

🔭 Turning the Telescope: Implementing Enforced Leanness

If the browser won't be aggressive, your extension will be. By enforcing a "hard ceiling" on active tabs, you ensure that you only ever hold a small batch of live tabs in your hand at once.

To achieve the telescope layout, your dashboard and background logic will follow a strict rule set:

1. The Hard Working Memory Cap (Tier 1 Constraint)

You set a hard configuration limit—for example, maximum 8 live tabs allowed in RAM at once.

  • If you open a 9th tab, the extension instantly runs a check on your current active group.
  • It finds the tab with the lowest engagement score that isn't currently focused, grabs its state, caches it to local storage, and executes chrome.tabs.discard().
  • The tab remains perfectly visible in your workspace layout, but Chrome is forced to clear its V8 engine heap entirely.

2. Context-Driven Swapping

Because you want to manage multiple large projects over months without context bleed, swapping between projects acts like changing the lens on the telescope:

  • When you switch from your H1: "Embedded Prototyping" project to your H1: "Systems Engineering Coursework" project, the extension handles the heavy lifting instantly.
  • It completely discards or closes all 8 tabs from the first project (saving their exact hierarchical structure, scroll positions, and states into the local database).
  • It then pulls the high-priority nodes from the second project out of "cold storage" and loads only its top 3 or 4 primary tabs back into active memory.

This approach gives you the ultimate best of both worlds: your physical machine runs flawlessly with an incredibly lean memory footprint, while your visual dashboard preserves an infinite canvas of your intellectual rabbit holes over the last several months.

turns.response_html:
This is the breakthrough the architecture needs. Mapping one Window to exactly one Bundle (with one Focus) matches perfectly with how modern operating systems handle window management (like virtual desktops or spaces).

By using the browser window as the physical boundary for a single context, you can seamlessly scale to multiple projects without any context bleed.

Let's break down the mechanics of the Bundle Aging Pipeline and exactly how the visual fidelity decays at each layer.

🧊 The 4-Layer Thermal Storage Architecture

As a project cools down, its visual complexity and data footprint shrink, naturally decluttering your visual field.

[ LIVE BUNDLE ]  --> 1 Active Window = 1 Focused Project. 
  │                  Full visual high-fidelity. Max 8 tabs loaded in RAM.
  ▼ (User changes focus / Closes window)
[ THE INACTIVE POOL ] -> Swapped out. Window is closed.
  │                      Stored as a full, rich tree map in the Sidepanel/Dashboard.
  ▼ (1 Day Inactive)
[ THE FRIDGE ]   --> Cold Storage. Stored as a streamlined outliner text layout.
  │                  Metadata only. Sub-groups collapsed. Low-score tabs hidden.
  ▼ (1 Week Inactive)
[ THE FREEZER ]  --> Deep Freezing. Compressed into a macro-view metadata string.
                     Visualized purely as high-level data metrics or timeline blocks.

Layer 1: The Live Bundle (The Hand)

  • The UI Experience: A dedicated Chrome window. The extension uses a sidebar panel to show the active H1–H6 tree structure.
  • The Constraint: A strict cap on active RAM. If you have 20 tabs in this bundle, only the 5–8 most recently used ones are alive; the rest are instantly hibernated using chrome.tabs.discard().

Layer 2: The Inactive Pool (The Desk)

  • The UI Experience: You decide to stop working on a project for the afternoon. You "stash" the bundle. The extension closes the entire Chrome window to clear your desktop and system memory.
  • The Visual Fidelity: High. If you open your main extension dashboard, this bundle is still rendered as a full, rich interactive map. You can see tab titles, favicons, custom notes, and exact hierarchies. It's ready to be hot-swapped back into a live window with one click.

Layer 3: The Fridge (Cold Storage — 1 Day Inactive)

  • The UI Experience: The bundle hasn't been touched in 24 hours. The extension automatically moves it from the active pool into the Fridge.
  • The Visual Fidelity Loss: The UI strips away the noise. Favicons disappear to reduce visual clutter. All sub-groups (H3–H6) are automatically collapsed under their parent H2 headers. Low-engagement tabs (pages you opened but spent less than 30 seconds on) are hidden behind a grayed-out "+ X more unread tabs" utility link. It reads like a clean, high-level text outline.

Layer 4: The Freezer (Deep Freezing — 1 Week Inactive)

  • The UI Experience: The bundle has been neglected for a week. It drops into the Freezer.
  • The Visual Fidelity Loss: Radical compression. Individual tabs are completely hidden from standard view. The bundle is represented purely as a macro-data summary card on your long-term timeline.

🔁 The Hot-Swapping Engine Logic

To make bundles feel "hot-swappable" across multiple windows, the extension needs to map Chrome's native windowId to your custom bundle structures.

When you click "Launch Bundle" from your dashboard:

  1. The extension calls chrome.windows.create({ focused: true }).
  2. It captures the newly created window.id.
  3. It queries your local database for that bundle's saved tree structure.
  4. It opens only the top-level high-priority tabs into that window, immediately assigning them their hierarchical tags in the sidebar.

This telescope approach guarantees that your physical system remains lightweight and incredibly fast, even if you have 500 tabs spanning months sitting in the Freezer.
